rationale: A wins because it finds the cleanest, least self-serving story in the launch: "A blood-pressure feature that needs a blood-pressure cuff to work." B is competent, but "Whoop finally gets FDA-cleared ECG — and bets the next fight is blood pressure" and "Cuffless blood pressure is the next wearable battleground" circle the same ECG-table-stakes/BP-frontier idea. A gives the founder more distinct lanes and harder proof questions, which is where angles stop being brainstorm filler and start becoming pitchable.
gaps_in_A: "blood pressure — a feature nobody has cleared" is not in the update; the facts only say competitors already ship FDA-cleared ECG.
"company whose entire model is subscription rather than hardware margin" imports business-model context not supplied; stick to the supplied top-tier gating unless sourced.
"Health reporters are actively covering wearable-accuracy gaps" is a live-beat claim without a supplied news signal; instinct is not evidence.
"newsjack-detector" as the next step may be overbuilt if the launch itself is the peg; for a proof-ready angle, journalist fit-check is the faster move.
gaps_in_B: "Whoop finally gets FDA-cleared ECG" and "late to ECG" need the competitor timeline before they become headline-safe.
"the average wearer can't tell the difference" invents user confusion; ask whether the labeling makes the distinction clear instead of asserting it.

"Whoop finally gets FDA-cleared ECG — and bets the next fight is blood pressure" and "Cuffless blood pressure is the next wearable battleground" are too close; one should become the sharper cuff-calibration accountability story.
"Cuffless blood pressure" is a little cute for a feature that explicitly requires cuff calibration; don't let the headline outrun the caveat.
